name: Unity Version Control

status.note: Called Plastic SCM until Unity rebranded it in 2023; plasticscm.com now points to Unity DevOps.

summary: Unity’s version control system, formerly Plastic SCM: one repository that programmers can use distributed, with branches and push and pull, while artists check files in straight to the server and lock what they can’t merge.
intro: A Unity Version Control (UVCS) server, in Unity’s cloud or on your own machines, holds repositories of changesets, branches and labels. The same repository supports two ways of working. Centralized, a workspace talks directly to the server: you check out only the files you need and check in straight to it, with no local copy of the repository. Distributed, you replicate a repository to your machine and push and pull branches like in Git; a `nodata` replica copies all the changesets, branches and permissions but none of the file contents, which it downloads on demand. Xlinks split a large project into several repositories, so code can be fully replicated while a big art repository stays central.

It is built around game teams’ binary assets. Gluon is a separate client for people who work on one branch with files that can’t be merged, such as images, animations and documents: they pick just the files they need, lock them, and never deal with branches. Smart Locks make locks follow branches: if you check in a locked file on a task branch, the lock stays “retained” until the change is merged to the destination branch (`/main` by default), so nobody else starts from an outdated revision. GitSync can push to and pull from any Git server over `https://` or `git://`. Unity says it works with any engine, Unreal included.

Códice Software in Spain released it as Plastic SCM in 2006; Unity bought Códice in August 2020 and rebranded the product in 2023, and it is now part of Unity DevOps alongside Build Automation. Since March 1, 2026, the public cloud service has had no per-seat charges: the first 25 GB of storage per organization each month is free, then $0.14 per GB-month, and 100 GB of egress a month is free, then $0.10 per GB. On-premises and legacy Plastic SCM licences may have different terms. The latest release is 11.0.16.10484 (October 15, 2026).
strengths: Distributed and centralized work in one repository: programmers branch and push, artists check in directly without a local repository
Locking designed for binary assets: Gluon for artists, and Smart Locks that track a locked file across branches until it is merged
Partial history: `nodata` replicas and Xlinks avoid downloading every revision of large art repositories
No per-seat charges on the public cloud since March 2026, with 25 GB of storage a month free
limits: Proprietary and controlled by Unity, and its pricing has changed often: the free cloud tier went from 3 seats and 5 GB in 2020 to unlimited seats and 25 GB in 2026
Egress beyond 100 GB a month is billed, which adds up for teams syncing large assets
A much smaller ecosystem than Git; GitSync bridges the two, but means running both systems
A `nodata` replica still needs the central server to fetch file contents until they are downloaded

snippet.title: Work on a task branch with the cm command line
source: cd ~/mygame && cm update                      # get the latest files
cm sync mygame@myorganization@cloud git https://github.com/acme/mygame.git   # exchange changes with Git

story: In late 2004 a group of engineers in Spain saw a gap in version control. Large teams used ClearCase and small teams used Subversion. They wanted a system built for feature branches and task branches that a team of 20 or fewer could afford. Pablo Santos co-founded Códice Software in 2005 to build it, and Plastic SCM 1.0 was unveiled in November 2006 at Microsoft’s TechEd Developers event in Barcelona. The core was written in C#, for productivity, with Mono running clients and servers on Mac and Linux.

Plastic was fully distributed but could also work centrally, with clients connected straight to a server, so both styles could coexist in one team. In 2013 GitSync let it push to and pull from Git servers such as GitHub directly over Git’s own protocols. Version 6.0 in 2017 introduced Jet, its own repository storage, alongside the SQL databases it had used before.

On August 17, 2020, Unity announced it had acquired Códice. It positioned Plastic for larger teams that needed branching, locking and merging, promised continued support for people who didn’t use the Unity engine, and added a free tier for up to three users. In 2023 Unity rebranded Plastic SCM as Unity Version Control, part of Unity DevOps, and in March 2026 it dropped per-seat charges for the cloud service.

choices.choice: Branch per task from the start
choices.why: When many considered branches harmful, Plastic’s founders made creating branches fast and cheap so any team could give every task its own branch, at a time when many version control developers considered branches harmful.

choices.choice: Distributed and centralized in one product
choices.why: Enterprises worried about every developer holding a full clone. Plastic let each user choose: replicate and push and pull, keep only partial replicas, or skip the local repository and check in straight to the server.
Santos chose C# for productivity, simpler code and ease of learning, and relied on Mono to run the same clients and servers on Mac and Linux.

Artists work on a single branch with files that can’t be merged and don’t want to download a huge repository for one or two files. Gluon lets them select just those files and lock them, and leaves branching and merging to others.
